frozen_original.title: Ramaswamy Strive Anti-ESG Fund Serves Fossil Fuel Investor Class While Running for Governor
frozen_original.synopsis: Strive Asset Management — Ramaswamy co-founded 2022 with $30M from Peter Thiel and conservative financiers — structured as explicit counter to ESG investing, advocating corporations maximize profits without climate, diversity, or governance considerations. Attracted significant fossil fuel funding. Holds stakes in major corporations, uses shareholder position to oppose sustainability commitments and climate disclosures. In Ohio governor race, fund has interests in energy companies affected by state environmental regulation. Platform emphasis on making Ohio "top state to start and grow a business" aligns with Strive investor preferences — conflict between fiduciary duties to investors and prospective duty to Ohio citizens near industrial sites. Also remains significant Roivant Sciences shareholder with multiple FDA drugs in review.
frozen_original.rationale: Business empire built on pharmaceutical arbitrage (Roivant) and anti-regulation advocacy (Strive) creates concrete conflicts if he becomes governor. Political persona as outsider obscures deep corporate establishment embedding. DOGE association provided political cover for leading governor race despite zero governing experience.

frozen_original.title: Trump Fires CISA Director Jen Easterly and All Cyber Security Board Members
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump fired Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Director Jen Easterly along with all members of the Cyber Safety Review Board, which had been investigating major cyberattacks including the Salt Typhoon intrusion into U.S. telecom networks. The firings halted an active investigation into one of the worst foreign hacks in American history, with the CSRB's report on Salt Typhoon never completed or released. Cybersecurity experts warned that firing the nation's top cyber defenders at the start of a term left critical infrastructure exposed. The move was widely condemned as leaving America more vulnerable to Chinese and Russian cyberattacks at a critical moment.

primary.title: DHS Ends CSRB Memberships; Easterly's Departure Is a Separate Claim
primary.description_short: DHS Ends CSRB Memberships; Easterly's Departure Is a Separate Claim
primary.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, DHS Acting Secretary Benjamine Huffman terminated current advisory-committee memberships, including the Cyber Safety Review Board, while it was investigating Salt Typhoon. The supplied record also says CISA Director Jen Easterly left at the presidential transition, but the accessible evidence does not establish a firing or connect her departure to the DHS memo. The combined entry remains an internal, unverified draft.
primary.description_long: This internal reconstruction separates two claims that the frozen entry joined. SANS and TechTarget report that a January 20 memo from Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman terminated advisory committee memberships, including the Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB), while it was examining the Salt Typhoon telecom intrusion. Those sources support a discrete DHS advisory-board action. The supplied packet separately says CISA Director Jen Easterly's tenure ended at the presidential transition. It supplies no direct source for her departure date or mechanism; the CISA leadership page retrieved in this session is a current directory and does not establish a January 2025 dismissal. Nothing accessed shows that Trump dismissed Easterly through the DHS memo, that her departure halted the CSRB inquiry, or that all federal cyber defense work stopped. The two issues therefore need separate records. This draft keeps the DHS action as a sourced child and treats the CISA departure as unverified supplied input. The frozen entry's claims about an unfinished report, critical-infrastructure exposure, and broad expert condemnation are not reproduced as established results. Keep the compound item internal until the separate departure claim is sourced.

By Alexander Culafi, Senior News Writer, Dark Reading. Published: 27 Jan 2025. Former members of the Department of Homeland Security's Cyber Safety Review Board have been broadly silent on their dismissals last week. Benjamine C. Huffman, who was the acting DHS secretary prior to Kristi Noem's confirmation Saturday, sent a Jan. 20 memo that immediately terminated all current DHS advisory committee memberships. Though not named in the memo directly, this included the Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB), an advisory board established by former President Joe Biden in 2021 to review and report on significant cybersecurity issues and incidents.

corrected_proposal.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman ended current advisory-committee memberships, including the Cyber Safety Review Board, SANS and TechTarget reported. The board was investigating the 2024 Salt Typhoon telecom intrusion. The sources establish the membership action, but do not show whether the review stopped or what security effects followed.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, Acting Department of Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued a memo ending current memberships on DHS advisory committees. SANS and TechTarget reported that the Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB) was included. The CSRB reviews significant cybersecurity incidents and makes recommendations; SANS noted that it had previously examined Log4Shell, Lapsus$ attacks, and the Microsoft Exchange Online breach. At the time of the memo, the board was investigating the 2024 Salt Typhoon intrusion into U.S. telecommunications networks. The reported action ended committee memberships while that review was underway. The sources do not establish whether the investigation stopped permanently, whether the board later resumed work, or what security effects followed. They also do not show that President Trump signed the memo or that the action caused CISA Director Jen Easterly’s separate departure at the presidential transition. This record concerns the membership termination and the contemporaneous review, not a halt to all federal cyber defense work or a measured cybersecurity loss.

source_fact_map.quote: An internal memo issued January 20, 2025, from Acting Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Benjamine Huffman, terminated all advisory committee positions. Among those dismissed were the Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB)
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: An internal memo issued January 20, 2025, from Acting Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Benjamine Huffman, terminated all advisory committee positions. Among those dismissed were the Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB), a committee responsible for “study[ing] major cyber incidents and recommend[ing] improvements,” comprising private sector experts and government cybersecurity officials. Since its establishment in 2022 by President Biden's executive order, the CSRB investigated the Log4Shell security crisis, attacks by Lapsus$, and the Microsoft Exchange Online Breach, and at the time of Huffman's memo was in the process of investigating the massive 2024 breach of US telecommunications networks by the Chinese state-sponsored hacking group, Salt Typhoon.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: The Cyber Safety Review Board was investigating recent attacks by Chinese state-sponsored threat actor Salt Typhoon when DHS terminated all advisory board memberships. By Alexander Culafi, Senior News Writer, Dark Reading. Published: 27 Jan 2025. Former members of the Department of Homeland Security's Cyber Safety Review Board have been broadly silent on their dismissals last week. Benjamine C. Huffman, who was the acting DHS secretary prior to Kristi Noem's confirmation Saturday, sent a Jan. 20 memo that immediately terminated all current DHS advisory committee memberships. Though not named in the memo directly, this included the Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB), an advisory board established by former President Joe Biden in 2021 to review and report on significant cybersecurity issues and incidents.

frozen_original.title: Trump Personally Attacks Supreme Court Justices Sotomayor and Jackson
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, President Trump launched personal attacks on Supreme Court Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson — the Court's two most liberal justices — posting on Truth Social that they should recuse themselves from all cases involving his administration, calling them 'radical left justices' and implying their rulings were motivated by racism and political bias rather than law. The attacks on sitting Supreme Court justices were described by legal scholars as an extraordinary breach of constitutional norms, with no parallel in modern American history. Former Chief Justices' clerks and judicial ethics experts noted the attacks were designed to either intimidate the justices into changing their votes or to delegitimize them in public opinion to soften the impact of adverse Supreme Court rulings. The attacks came while multiple emergency applications from the administration were pending before the Court, raising serious concerns about the administration's willingness to pressure sitting justices.

primary.title: Trump Demands Sotomayor and Ginsburg Recuse from Trump-Related Cases
primary.description_short: On Feb. 25, 2020, Trump called for Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg to recuse from Trump-related matters.
primary.description_medium: On Feb. 25, 2020, Trump demanded that Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg recuse from all Trump-related matters. ABC News tied the demand to criticism of Sotomayor's dissent in a case involving an administration policy. The supplied entry misdates the event to 2025, substitutes Ketanji Brown Jackson for Ginsburg, and adds an unsupported racism claim.
primary.description_long:
ABC News reported that on February 25, 2020, President Donald Trump called for two Supreme Court justices to recuse themselves from all Trump-related matters. He named Sonia Sotomayor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg and wrote, “Both should recuse themselves on all Trump, or Trump related, matters!” The article placed the demand after Sotomayor criticized the Court’s handling of a Trump administration policy and reported that Trump said the justices had treated him unfairly.

This is a public demand directed at sitting justices. The source does not establish that either justice recused in response, that the Court changed its procedures, or that a case outcome changed because of the statement. ABC also notes that justices decide for themselves when recusal is appropriate.

The supplied entry’s February 2025 date and reference to Ketanji Brown Jackson do not match the documented event: the source identifies Ruth Bader Ginsburg and dates the demand to February 25, 2020. The source supports a recusal demand and an accusation of unfair treatment; it does not support the separate claim that Trump accused the justices of racism. This repair describes the reported demand without implying that it caused a ruling or actual recusal.
